title: Checkpoint: Constitutions and Rights
objective: After this level you can explain how constitutions protect rights and how rights grew.
summary: South Africa's 1996 Constitution, signed at Sharpeville on Human Rights Day, gathers the chapter: a supreme law with a Bill of Rights for religion, privacy, the vote and equality.

cards.headline: In 1996 Nelson Mandela signed a constitution at the scene of a massacre.
cards.body: In 1960, at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a crowd demonstrating against apartheid's pass laws. On 10 December 1996, President Mandela signed South Africa's new constitution into law in the same place. The date was International Human Rights Day, the anniversary of Level 34's Declaration, adopted on 10 December 1948.

cards.headline: This chapter, inside one Bill of Rights

items.label: Belief and privacy
points: A right to privacy, including not having your home searched

items.label: The vote
points: Every adult citizen may vote, by secret ballot

items.label: Equality
points: No unfair discrimination on grounds including race, sex, religion, age and disability

cards.headline: Supreme, and meant to be
cards.body: The constitution is one written document of 14 chapters, and Chapter 2 is the Bill of Rights, which calls itself "a cornerstone of democracy in South Africa." Section 2 goes further: the Constitution is the supreme law, and "law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid." That's Level 31's idea with teeth. Under apartheid, the pass laws were law. Under this constitution, a law that discriminated unfairly by race would clash with the Bill of Rights, and so be invalid.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: What a constitution does as supreme law: it sets up government, limits power and protects rights.
Why constitutions are made harder to change than ordinary laws, and the risks of too rigid or too loose.
Why belief can't be limited but religious practice can, and how privacy grew to cover your data.
How the right to vote widened step by step, and why civil rights usually need government to act.

questions.prompt: Why does section 2 of South Africa's constitution matter so much after apartheid?

options.label: It kept the old pass laws in force
options.rationale: Section 2 makes laws inconsistent with the constitution invalid.

options.label: Any law inconsistent with the constitution is invalid
It lets Parliament set aside the Bill of Rights
options.rationale: The Constitution, including the Bill of Rights, is supreme over ordinary laws.

options.label: It makes the constitution impossible to amend
options.rationale: Supremacy is about which law wins, not about amending.

questions.explanation: Section 2 makes the Constitution the supreme law: law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid. Apartheid had worked through laws; now laws must fit the Bill of Rights.

questions.prompt: South Africa's constitution is one written document. Which country from Level 31 has a constitution that's a collection of statutes, documents and practices?

options.label: The United States
options.rationale: The U.S. Constitution is one specific written document.

options.label: South Africa
options.rationale: South Africa's is a single document of 14 chapters.

options.label: The United Kingdom
India
options.rationale: India changes its constitution by numbered amendments, like the 73rd.

questions.explanation: The UK's constitution is a collection of documents, statutes and traditional practices, not one written document.
